fonds-investissement-pme.label: SME investment funds
fonds-investissement-pme.title: SME investment funds in Belgium: 9 players compared
fonds-investissement-pme.excerpt: Nine funds and public invests active in Wallonia and Brussels, ranked on ticket size, instruments and exit horizon, as published on 15.10.2026.
fonds-investissement-pme.intro:
For an established Walloon SME looking for €500,000 to €2.5M without giving up control, I put ORSA (formerly Investsud) first, ahead of the provincial invests, then Wallonie Entreprendre, finance&invest.brussels and Theodorus. This ranking compares nine players on what they publish themselves: ticket size, instruments, exit horizon and area. All data was collected from their own websites on 15.10.2026; anything they do not publish is marked "not published".

Disclosure: this site features ORSA, and I rank it first. I justify that with verifiable facts that ORSA publishes itself: an evergreen fund with no imposed exit date, equity or quasi-equity on offer, and a ticket of €500,000 to €2,500,000 designed for SMEs of 20 to 150 people. None of the players listed reviewed this ranking, and none paid to appear at any rank other than its own.

An investment fund does not publish a price. What changes a business owner's life is the share of capital they give up, the moment the investor will want to sell, and the seat it takes on the board. That is what this ranking is about.
tldr: ORSA comes first for a Walloon SME of 20 to 150 people: evergreen, equity or a non-dilutive subordinated loan (Smart Bond), published ticket of €500,000 to €2.5M.
The provincial invests (Namur Invest, Invest.BW, Sambrinvest, Noshaq, IMBC) are the best door below €500,000 or for local roots, but each covers only one province or sub-region.
Wallonie Entreprendre combines loans, guarantees and equity for region-wide deals; finance&invest.brussels invests up to €5M in Brussels SMEs, alongside banks and private funds.
For a deep tech spin-off at seed stage, Theodorus invests from €250,000 — a different job from funding an established SME.

sections.q: Why does ORSA top this ranking?
sections.body:
Because it ticks the four criteria that matter most to an established SME: no imposed exit date, a choice between equity and quasi-equity, a published ticket, and coverage of all of Wallonia. It is neither the largest Walloon player nor the only one offering subordinated loans.

ORSA describes itself as an open-ended, evergreen fund: exit remains a normal step, but its timing is set with the company rather than by the lifespan of a fund vehicle. Its Smart Bond is a 5-to-10-year subordinated loan combining a minimum annual interest rate with a performance-linked component, typically tied to EBITDA, paid at maturity. The owner keeps 100% of the capital.

The published ticket runs from €500,000 to €2,500,000, with explicit criteria: Walloon industrial SMEs with 20 to 150 staff for growth, buyouts and succession; start-ups, scale-ups and biotechs rooted in Wallonia for innovation. Active since 1985 under the Investsud name, ORSA reports more than 300 companies backed and more than €120M under management.

Its limit is clear: it is not the right door for needs below €500,000, nor for a company without significant activity in Wallonia.

sections.q: What does a provincial invest offer that a regional fund does not?
sections.body:
Proximity and, often, smaller tickets. Namur Invest says it usually invests from €100,000 up to €2.5M; Invest.BW goes up to €2.5M in total, in one or several rounds, over 5 to 10 years.

The invests are public-private partnerships or commercial companies part-owned by the Walloon Region through Wallonie Entreprendre. Namur Invest, for example, is 60% private and 40% Region-owned. They assess return and risk like private investors, but their local development mission makes them open to smaller deals.

The catch is geography: a Liège SME goes to Noshaq, a Charleroi SME to Sambrinvest, an SME from Mons, the Borinage or the Centre region to IMBC. An excellent invest from another province will not fund you.

sections.q: Which player should a Brussels company approach?
sections.body:
finance&invest.brussels, the public financing arm of the Brussels-Capital Region, is the first port of call: it invests up to €5M in SMEs, alongside banks and private funds, and offers smaller loans through its brusoc subsidiary.

The Walloon invests and ORSA do not invest in companies without significant activity in Wallonia. A Brussels SME with a production site in Wallonia, however, can knock on both doors; this is common in Walloon Brabant.

sections.q: Can several funds join the same round?
sections.body:
Yes, and it is often the norm. Invest.BW states that it never funds the entire need on its own. A €2M package can combine a provincial invest in equity, a private fund with a subordinated loan and the bank with an investment loan, each with its own instrument.

The subordinated loan acts as leverage here: the bank counts it as quasi-equity, which improves the solvency ratio it looks at before granting its own credit. That is why I always check whether a player offers this kind of instrument before looking at its ticket.

sections.q: What should you check before signing with a fund?
sections.body:
Four questions, to ask before the letter of intent, not after. Who decides, and in how many steps: a single investment committee moves faster than a double approval. How long does the investor plan to stay: ask explicitly, even an evergreen fund. What seat on the board: a director's seat or an observer is common when a fund takes equity. And which exit clauses: drag-along, tag-along, ratchet.

For a loan, a fifth question matters: is it truly subordinated to bank debt? That is what allows your bank to treat it as quasi-equity.

criteria: Exit horizon: a closed-end fund must sell before its term; an evergreen fund or a long-horizon invest lets the owner choose the moment.
Instruments: equity for owners who want a partner, quasi-equity (subordinated or convertible loans) for those who do not want to open their capital; offering both covers more situations.
A ticket suited to SMEs of 20 to 150 people: from €500,000 to a few million, too much for a business angel, too little for a large private equity fund.
Area covered: a player active across Wallonia suits more companies than an invest limited to one province.
Transparency: published tickets, eligibility criteria and instruments tell an owner before the first meeting whether the deal stands a chance.
fonds-investissement-pme.methodology: All data comes from the players' official websites, read on 15.10.2026. No figure was taken from another comparison site or estimated; anything not published is marked "not published". I did not submit a file to each of them: this ranking compares published terms, not fundraising experiences. The rank reflects fit with the most common situation on this site — an established Walloon SME seeking €500,000 to €2.5M — not the absolute quality of a player.

faq.q: Does an investment fund always take a majority stake?
faq.a: No. The Walloon invests and funds such as ORSA usually invest as minority shareholders alongside the owner. Majority stakes are mostly found in buyouts (LBOs) led by larger private equity funds.

faq.q: What is the minimum amount to interest a fund?
faq.a: It depends on the player. Namur Invest usually invests from €100,000, Theodorus from €250,000 on a first investment, ORSA from €500,000. Below €100,000, regional loans, business angels and crowdfunding are often a better fit.

faq.q: Is a public fund less demanding than a private one?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The invests have a regional development mission, but they assess return and risk like private investors. The differences lie mainly in area, instruments and holding period.

faq.q: How long does it take to get a decision?
faq.a: None of the players reviewed publishes a firm timeline. Namur Invest says it depends on the amount, the type of investment and how mature the file is. Expect several weeks for a first decision, longer for closing including due diligence.

faq.q: Do you need an adviser to approach a fund?
faq.a: It is not mandatory. For a first raise of a few hundred thousand euros, many owners approach their provincial invest directly. An adviser becomes useful for valuation, the letter of intent and the shareholders' agreement.

faq.q: Does a subordinated loan dilute the owner?
faq.a: No, as long as it is not convertible. ORSA's Smart Bond, for instance, is a 5-to-10-year loan whose return partly depends on EBITDA: the owner keeps 100% of the capital.

The site features ORSA and says so at the top of the page. ORSA's rank is justified by its published terms; the other players' data comes from their own websites, and none of them reviewed the ranking.

invests-wallons.label: Walloon invests
invests-wallons.title: Walloon invests: the 9 provincial investment companies compared
invests-wallons.excerpt: The nine Walloon invests, from Noshaq to Wapinvest, ranked on what they publish: ticket, instruments, term and area, dated at the time of reading.
invests-wallons.intro:
For a Walloon SME looking for equity or a subordinated loan from an invest, I put ORSA (formerly Investsud) first, ahead of Namur Invest and Invest.BW, because those three publish a ticket and instruments you can check. Noshaq and Carbon (formerly Sambrinvest) come next: the largest portfolios in Wallonia, but no published ticket. Wapinvest, Ostbelgieninvest, IMBC and Luxembourg Développement close the list, not because they finance less well, but because they tell you less before the first meeting.

Wallonia has nine invests, one per main economic area, most of them created in the 1980s. An invest is an investment company with public and private shareholders, in which the Region holds a stake through Wallonie Entreprendre (WE, the Walloon public financing agency), and which finances companies in its area with equity and loans. The Walloon government confirmed to Parliament on 12 May 2025 that their capital is mostly private, Noshaq being the exception.

One limit to state up front: this ranking does not move you to another province. An SME in Tournai goes to Wapinvest, an SME in Eupen to Ostbelgieninvest, whatever their rank here. The rank measures the quality of the published information and the breadth of instruments, not the odds of a given application. ORSA is the partner featured by this site; its rank rests on conditions it publishes itself, and no invest reviewed this ranking. Data read on the invests' websites on 15.10.2026 (ORSA, Namur Invest, Invest.BW, Noshaq, IMBC) and on 28.10.2026 (Carbon, Wapinvest, Ostbelgieninvest, Luxembourg Développement).
tldr: Nine invests cover Wallonia, one per area: your operating site decides which one is yours long before this ranking does.
Only three publish a ticket: ORSA (€500,000 to €2.5M), Namur Invest (€100,000 to €2.5M as a rule) and Invest.BW (up to €2.5M in total); Wapinvest publishes a €15,000 floor.
Noshaq commits €120M a year on average and Carbon, Sambrinvest's new name since 20.10.2026, announces €220M of projects by 2029: high volume, no published ticket.
An invest lends more than it invests: about 80% debt at Namur Invest, subordinated loans of up to 10 years at Ostbelgieninvest, a 5 to 10-year Smart Bond at ORSA.

sections.body:
The one where your operating site is, almost always. The invests split Wallonia into areas, and each requires the company to be established there or to commit to setting up there.

The split published as of 28.10.2026: Noshaq for the province of Liège; Carbon for the 30 municipalities of Charleroi Métropole; Namur Invest for the province of Namur; Invest.BW for Walloon Brabant; IMBC for Mons, the Borinage and the Centre; Wapinvest for the districts of Mouscron, Tournai and Ath, plus Lessines, Enghien and Silly; Ostbelgieninvest for the nine German-speaking municipalities and seven neighbouring Liège municipalities (Plombières, Welkenraedt, Baelen, Malmedy, Waimes, Stavelot, Trois-Ponts); Luxembourg Développement, based in Arlon, for the province of Luxembourg. ORSA, based in Marche-en-Famenne, publishes an area of intervention covering the whole of Wallonia.

Two cases deserve a check. An SME in Malmedy or Welkenraedt can knock on Noshaq's door and on Ostbelgieninvest's. And an SME with its registered office in Brussels but its plant in Wavre falls under Invest.BW for the Walloon site, and under finance&invest.brussels for the rest.

sections.q: Why do only three invests publish a ticket?
sections.body:
Because the amount is decided case by case, and an invest would rather not set a ceiling it will exceed by co-investing. Yet it is the piece of information that saves you a meeting.

ORSA publishes €500,000 to €2,500,000. Namur Invest announces €100,000 to €2.5M as a rule, and says it also invests below €500,000. Invest.BW caps at €2.5M in total, in one or several rounds: take €1M today and €1.5M remains for later. Wapinvest publishes no ceiling but a €15,000 intervention floor, the lowest in the panel. Noshaq, Carbon, IMBC, Ostbelgieninvest and Luxembourg Développement: not published.

Without a ticket, volumes give an order of magnitude. Noshaq commits €120M of investments a year on average over five years. Wapinvest accepted 133 applications in 2024 for €33.9M, or about €255,000 per application on average. I calculated that from its annual report: an average is not a ticket, but it tells you which range of amounts the invest works in most often.

sections.q: Does an invest take equity or lend?
sections.body:
It lends more often than it takes equity. Namur Invest reports a portfolio split roughly 20% equity and 80% debt, with three to four interventions per company on average over time.

The published range varies a lot from one invest to the next. Namur Invest lists equity stakes, convertible, subordinated, unsecured, secured and bullet loans, and real estate leasing. Ostbelgieninvest describes four instruments: a minority, time-limited stake whose exit is set in the contract from the start, a subordinated loan of up to 10 years usually without collateral, a short-term loan of 3 months to 3 years, and a convertible bond. Luxembourg Développement announces fixed-rate loans and equity interventions. IMBC does not detail its instruments on the pages consulted.

For the owner, the difference is counted in points of capital. €300,000 of subordinated loan takes no stake. The same €300,000 in equity on a pre-money valuation of €900,000 costs you 25% (300,000 out of €1.2M post-money), plus a board member: Namur Invest writes that it usually asks for one when it takes equity.

Perhaps, which is a reason to ask who will decide on your file in two years' time. The regional policy statement aims to rationalise and reduce the number of invests; a parliamentary question of 16 April 2025 mentioned going from nine to four or five.

The Economy minister did not confirm that figure. His reply of 12 May 2025 says he will examine proposals coming from the invests themselves, that an evaluation of the agreements between the invests and Wallonie Entreprendre was planned for the end of 2025, and that ending advances to the invests would free €30M a year. Some invests might then look for new shareholders.

Recent renamings show a network on the move: Meusinvest became Noshaq, Nivelinvest became Invest.BW, Investsud became ORSA, and Sambrinvest took the name Carbon on 20 October 2026. If your shareholders' agreement runs for ten years, have it state what happens if the invest merges or transfers its stake to another entity.

sections.q: What should you ask an invest before signing?
sections.body:
Four things, in writing, before the letter of intent.

The realistic ticket for your file and the share of capital it represents under two or three valuations. The partner or partners it proposes to bring in: Invest.BW writes that it never finances the whole need alone, and most invests structure deals with the bank. The term and the exit: a subordinated loan has a maturity, an equity stake should have one too, and Ostbelgieninvest sets the exit in the contract at entry. The list of decisions subject to the invest's board member, to be negotiated in the shareholders' agreement before the price.

One last point applies to all of them: the invests exclude companies in difficulty. Wapinvest, for example, rules out those that have lost more than half of their capital. An SME in turnaround should first see its accountant, and a lawyer before signing anything.

criteria: Transparency: ticket, instruments and term published on the invest's website, checkable before the first meeting.
Breadth of instruments: equity, subordinated loan, convertible, short-term loan or leasing; the wider the range, the more situations the invest can serve.
Published financial capacity: annual volume invested, assets under management or number of applications accepted.
Size of the area: an invest covering a whole province serves more companies than one limited to a few districts.
Clarity of status: public and private shareholding, role of Wallonie Entreprendre, written eligibility conditions.
invests-wallons.methodology: Each entry reflects what the invest publishes on its website, in its annual report or in a press release, with the date it was read: 15.10.2026 for ORSA, Namur Invest, Invest.BW, Noshaq and IMBC, 28.10.2026 for Carbon, Wapinvest, Ostbelgieninvest and Luxembourg Développement. Sambrinvest's renaming to Carbon and its €220M plan come from the press of 20.10.2026 (La DH, Télésambre). Wapinvest's average per application is my calculation (€33.9M divided by 133 applications accepted in 2024). Information missing from the invest's site is marked "not published". I did not submit an application to any invest: the rank compares published information and breadth of instruments, not the quality of support. The score out of 100 weights transparency (35 points), range of instruments (25), published capacity (20), area (10) and clarity of status (10).

faq.q: How many invests are there in Wallonia?
faq.a: Nine: Noshaq, Carbon (formerly Sambrinvest), Namur Invest, Invest.BW, IMBC, Wapinvest, Ostbelgieninvest, Luxembourg Développement and ORSA (formerly Investsud). The Walloon government confirmed that number to Parliament in May 2025, while aiming to streamline the network.

faq.q: Can you approach the invest of another province?
faq.a: As a rule, no: each invest finances companies established in its area or committing to set up there. ORSA publishes an area covering the whole of Wallonia, and Ostbelgieninvest can work elsewhere in cooperation with the other invests.

faq.q: What is the minimum amount for an invest?
faq.a: Wapinvest publishes a €15,000 intervention floor. Namur Invest usually invests from €100,000, ORSA from €500,000. The other invests publish no minimum: ask before you build the file.

Under another name. Sambrinvest became Carbon on 20 October 2026, with the same area (the 30 municipalities of Charleroi Métropole) and an announced target of €220M of projects by 2029. Its managing director is Grégoire Dupuis.

faq.q: Is an invest a public body?
faq.a: It is a company with mixed shareholding. Wapinvest is 60% privately held and 40% held by Wallonie Entreprendre, Namur Invest in the same proportion. Noshaq is the exception, with mostly public capital according to the minister.

faq.q: How long does an invest's subordinated loan last?
faq.a: Ostbelgieninvest publishes a term of up to 10 years with a jointly agreed repayment plan, ORSA a Smart Bond of 5 to 10 years. Invest.BW announces interventions of 5 to 10 years. The others publish no term.

This site features ORSA and says so in the introduction. ORSA's rank rests on conditions it publishes; the other entries come from the invests' own websites and reports, and none of them reviewed or paid for this ranking.
